A.explanation: It is wrong to split the 9 nucleons into 4 baryons and 5 mesons, as both protons and neutrons are baryons.

B.explanation: It is wrong to count 5 baryons and 4 mesons, as no mesons exist as stable constituents inside the $^{9}_{4}\text{Be}$ nucleus.

C.explanation: All 9 nucleons are baryons and all baryons are hadrons, so there are 9 hadrons, 9 baryons and 0 mesons.

D.explanation: The total cannot be 13, as hadrons in the nucleus are just the $4+5=9$ nucleons, not protons plus neutrons plus something else.

hints: Notice the nuclide notation $^{9}_{4}\text{Be}$ gives proton number $Z=4$ and nucleon number $A=9$, so work out the numbers of protons and neutrons.
Recall that protons and neutrons are both nucleons, both baryons made of three quarks, and both members of the hadron family.
Recall that mesons are a different hadron group made of quark-antiquark pairs and are not stable constituents of a nucleus, so decide how the 9 hadrons divide into baryons and mesons.
walkthrough: Read $^{9}_{4}\text{Be}$ as $Z=4$ protons and $A=9$ total nucleons, so neutrons $= A-Z = 9-4 = 5$.
The nucleus therefore contains $4$ protons $+$ $5$ neutrons $= 9$ nucleons in total.
State the particle rule: hadrons are particles made of quarks, divided into baryons with three quarks and mesons with one quark and one antiquark.
Protons ($uud$) and neutrons ($udd$) are both three-quark baryons, so all 9 nucleons are 9 baryons and hence 9 hadrons.
There are no stable mesons bound inside the nucleus, so meson count $= 0$.
That gives hadrons $= 9$, baryons $= 9$, mesons $= 0$. This is option C.
